The stepmother, angered by his refusal, conspires with a servant to poison him, but her own younger son drinks the poisoned wine and dies. It develops this through examples of fixed seeds, seasonal growth, cultivation, dissolution into primal bodies, and the replenishment of living kinds and cosmic bodies by eternal matter.","language":"English","quote_policy":"quoted"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The passage says terror and mental darkness are not dispersed by sunrise or morning light but by Nature's aspect and law.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The passage states the principle that nothing is born from nothing and that created things arise from elements rather than by tools of Gods.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Men are described as attributing unknown causes in land and sky to Divinities because fear holds dominion over mortality.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"A hypothetical disorder is described in which, if all things sprang from all things, men might rise from the sea, scaly creatures from land, and birds from the sky.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The passage asserts that produced things arise from fixed seeds, their own stuff, and their own primal bodies.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Seasonal examples include roses in spring, corn in summer heat, and vines maturing in autumn, with earth giving progenies at due times.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Growth is described as gradual: a babe does not immediately walk as a man, a branching tree does not leap from turf, and living things require proper matter, rain, and food.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The passage compares primal bodies common to many things with single letters common to many words.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Tilled fields surpass untilled fields, and the ploughshare is said to quicken primordial germs in the earth into birth.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Nature is said to dissolve all things back into primal bodies, while nothing perishes to annihilation.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Destruction of things is said to require an outward blow or an inward dissolving force acting on their bonds or hollow cells.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Venus is described as restoring generations kind by kind to the light of life, and daedal Earth as fostering them with ancient food.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Water-springs and inland rivers are described as keeping the ocean full, and Atoms collide, rebound, combine into dense bodies or rare forms, and visible motes in sunbeams serve as an analogy for hidden atomic world-stuff generate and later dissolve the varied world.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Matter is described as not cohering tightly; visible things wane as motes leave them and increase other things.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The total sum is said to remain replenished while mortals live by exchange, nations wax and wane, and generations pass life onward.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The primordial germs of things are said not to stop; they move through void by their own weight or by another body's blow.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Primordial bodies repeatedly meet, clash, and leap apart because they are hard and solid and have no resistance behind them.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The passage states that the whole has no bottom or realm of rest because space is unbounded and extends in every direction.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Some atoms rebound with small gaps and form dense things such as rocks and iron; others leave large gaps and supply thin air and sunlight.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Many other bodies are described as wandering the mighty void, cast back from unions and not linked with the motions of the rest.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Dust-like motes are visible in sunbeams entering dark halls, moving in many ways, contending, meeting, parting, and being driven up and down.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The visible tumbling of motes in light is presented as a sign of secret and invisible motions of primal stuff beneath or behind appearances.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Motion is described as beginning from primeval atoms, content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.roman-lucretius-nature-of-things-leonard-gutenberg-l2412-l2467","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/roman/project-gutenberg/on-the-nature-of-things-lucretius-leonard.md","passage_locator":{"label":"BOOK II / PROEM / ATOMIC MOTIONS / ATOMIC FORMS AND THEIR  COMBINATIONS; lines 2412-2467","start":"2412","end":"2467","translation":"On the Nature of Things","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage denies that all things can combine with all things, using impossible hybrid monsters as examples. It argues that living beings arise from fixed seed and dam, preserve ancestral type by fixed law, and assimilate only suitable atoms. It then extends such lawfulness to all things, explaining diversity through differently shaped atoms and using letters, words, and verses as an analogy for atomic combinations. It concludes that differing seeds, spaces, weights, blows, and motions distinguish living forms and separate ocean, land, and heaven.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The passage says that if all things could be conjoined in all ways, portents would appear on every side.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The imagined portents include half-brute human hulks, branches sprouting from a man's trunk, sea-beast limbs knit to a land-beast, and flame-breathing Chimaeras.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The passage states that such beings have not been begotten.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The passage says living beings are engendered from fixed seed and fixed dam and preserve their ancestral type during growth.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The passage describes eaten food as yielding atoms suited to each creature; these atoms pass through bodies, join there, and produce proper motions.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The passage says nature throws off atoms foreign to a creature's frame, and that some viewless bodies fly out or fail to join or take on vital motions.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The passage states that these laws bind not only living forms but all He compares the soul’s dissolution to liquids leaving broken jars and smoke or fog dispersing, and supports mortality by observing that mind develops, ages, suffers disease, is affected by wine, and is disrupted by bodily fits.","language":"English","quote_policy":"quoted"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The speaker says he will teach that the minds and light souls of living beings have mortal birth and death, and that mind and soul may be treated under one name because they are one interjoined substance.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The soul is described as a subtle fabric made of very minute particles, smaller than particles of liquid water, fog, or smoke, and more mobile than those substances.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The passage mentions sleepers seeing altars exhaling steam and smoke aloft, and says such apparitions come from outward.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Liquids are said to depart when jars are shivered, and fog and smoke are said to depart into the winds; the soul is likewise said to be shed abroad and dissolved back to primal bodies after leaving human members.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The body is compared to a jar-like container of the soul; when the body is shivered or rarefied by blood loss, it can no longer hold the soul.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Mind is said to come into being with the body, grow with the body, and age with the body: children have weak wisdom, maturity brings greater counsel, and old age brings failing thought, wandering tongue, and yielding mind.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The passage states that the body has diseases and dreadful pain, and the mind likewise has bitter cares, grief, and fear.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"In bodily diseases, the mind is said to wander, speak crazily, sink into heavy drowse and eternal sleep, and no brawls.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"A sudden fit is compared to a stroke of lightning: someone tumbles down, foams, grunts, blithers, twists with taut content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.roman-lucretius-nature-of-things-leonard-gutenberg-l3713-l3799","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/roman/project-gutenberg/on-the-nature-of-things-lucretius-leonard.md","passage_locator":{"label":"BOOK III / PROEM / NATURE AND COMPOSITION OF THE MIND / THE SOUL IS MORTAL; lines 3713-3799","start":"3713","end":"3799","translation":"On the Nature of Things","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage argues that mind and soul are mortal: disease can disturb them within the body, medicine can restore them, severed organs cannot function apart from the body, and the mind and body have vital powers only in their conjoined estate. After death, when bodily containment is lost and breath is forced out, the soul and the senses of the mind dissolve rather than live independently in air.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A diseased man is described as foaming, groaning, and having limbs gripped, with his condition compared to billows on the salt sea under winds.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The passage says the energy of mind and soul is confounded, split apart, and torn by venom during the disease.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"When the poison retreats, the man rises reeling and gradually recovers his senses and soul.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The passage states that great diseases shake the mind and soul within the human body, then questions whether they could live bodyless in open air battling winds.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The mind is said to be curable like the sick body and restorable by medicine.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The passage states that changing any nature requires adding parts, rearranging order, or removing some part.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The passage states that what is immortal does not allow its parts to be increased, rearranged, or diminished, and that change beyond its bounds means the death of what was before.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The mind is described as one part of a man, remaining in a fixed place like ears, eyes, and other senses.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"A severed hand, eye, or nose is said neither to feel nor be, and quickly rots.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The mind alone is said never to be able to exist without the body and the man himself; the body is compared to a vessel for the mind and is joined to it by strong bonds.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The live powers of body and mind are said to prosper and enjoy only in union.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The mind without body is said not to give vital motions, and the body without soul is said not to endure or use the senses.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"An eye uprooted from the body is said to be unable to see anything, and this is compared to soul and mind being unable when alone.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The elements of mind and soul are described as confined through veins, inward parts, bones, and sinews, and as taking on motions of sense while shut within bodily confines.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"After death, when thrown beyond the body into air and winds, the soul and mind are said to be unable to take on motions of sense because they are no longer bodily confined.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"When the body's wrappings are unwound and vital breath is forced out, the soul and the senses of the mind are said to dissolve.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"diseased man","description":"A man suffering a disease or poison, foaming, groaning, reeling, and later recovering his senses and soul.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"mind and soul","description":"The mind and soul are treated as a human life-principle affected by disease, medicine, bodily union, and dissolution after death.","role_refs":["role:2","role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:3","ev:4","ev:6","ev:7","ev:8"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"body of man","description":"The human body is described as the place, vessel, and confining structure in which mind and soul have sensory motions and live powers.","role_refs":["role:3","role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:5","ev:6","ev:7","ev:8"]}],"roles":[{"id":"role:1","label":"diseased patient","assigned_to":["fig:1"],"basis":"The man is shown in the symptoms of disease or poison and then in recovery.","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"role:2","label":"mortal life-principle under examination","assigned_to":["fig:2"],"basis":"The passage uses disease, cure, bodily dependence, and dissolution to argue for the mortality of mind and soul.","evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:4","ev:6","ev:8"]},{"id":"role:3","label":"bodily vessel and confining structure","assigned_to":["fig:3"],"basis":"The body is compared to a vessel for the mind, joined by bonds, and later described as confining the elements that permit sensory motions.","evidence_refs":["ev:5","ev:7"]},{"id":"role:4","label":"conjoined partners in life","assigned_to":["fig:2","fig:3"],"basis":"The body's and mind's live powers are said to prosper only in union, and the cause of life is their conjoined estate.","evidence_refs":["ev:6","ev:8"]}],"symbols":[{"id":"sym:1","label":"salt sea billows under winds","literal_form":"Billows on the salt sea boiling under the might of winds, used as a comparison for the diseased man's foaming.","associated_figures":["fig:1"],"taxonomy_refs":["water"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"sym:2","label":"winds and open air","literal_form":"Open air and winds, presented as the imagined place where a bodyless mind and soul would have to live and battle.","associated_figures":["fig:2"],"taxonomy_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:7"]},{"id":"sym:3","label":"medicine","literal_form":"Medicine that restores the sick body and mind.","associated_figures":["fig:2"],"taxonomy_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"sym:4","label":"body as vessel","literal_form":"The body described as the vessel of the mind or as something even more closely joined to it.","associated_figures":["fig:2","fig:3"],"taxonomy_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"sym:5","label":"severed organs","literal_form":"Hand, eye, or nose separated from the body; an uprooted eye unable to see.","associated_figures":["fig:3"],"taxonomy_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:5","ev:6"]},{"id":"sym:6","label":"body's wrappings and vital breath","literal_form":"The body's wrappings unwound and the vital breath forced out at death.","associated_figures":["fig:2","fig:3"],"taxonomy_refs":[],"evidence_refs":["ev:8"]}],"scenes":[{"id":"scene:1","label":"Disease, poison, and recovery","summary":"A diseased man foams and groans while mind and soul are described as torn by venom; when poison retreats, he reels upward and recovers senses and soul.","figure_refs":["fig:1","fig:2"],"symbol_refs":["sym:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2"]},{"id":"scene:2","label":"Argument from sickness, cure, and change","summary":"The speaker argues that mind and soul are shaken by bodily disease, can be cured by medicine, and therefore show mortality because change implies alteration of parts.","figure_refs":["fig:2"],"symbol_refs":["sym:2","sym:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:4"]},{"id":"scene:3","label":"Mind compared with bodily parts","summary":"The mind is treated as a part fixed in a man like the senses; severed organs cannot function apart from the body, so the mind cannot exist without body and man.","figure_refs":["fig:2","fig:3"],"symbol_refs":["sym:4","sym:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"scene:4","label":"Union in life and dissolution after death","summary":"Body and mind have live powers only in union; once bodily confinement is lost and vital breath is forced out, soul and mental senses dissolve.","figure_refs":["fig:2","fig:3"],"symbol_refs":["sym:2","sym:5","sym:6"],"evidence_refs":["ev:6","ev:7","ev:8"]}],"candidate_motifs":[{"id":"motif:1","label":"Disease and cure as proof of the mind's mortality","taxonomy_refs":[],"basis":"The passage presents disease as shaking mind and soul and medicine as restoring the mind, then explicitly treats this as a sign that the mind is mortal.","evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:4"],"confidence":"high","cautions":"This is a philosophical-poetic argument rather than a mythic narrative episode."},{"id":"motif:2","label":"Body as vessel or container of soul and mind","taxonomy_refs":[],"basis":"The body is compared to a vessel of the mind and later described as the bodily confinement that allows sensory motions.","evidence_refs":["ev:5","ev:7"],"confidence":"high","cautions":"The passage uses the vessel image for anatomy and psychology, not for a voyage or ark narrative."},{"id":"motif:3","label":"Body-mind duality sustained by union","taxonomy_refs":["duality"],"basis":"The passage distinguishes body, mind, and soul while saying their live powers prosper only in union and that life rests in their conjoined estate.","evidence_refs":["ev:6","ev:8"],"confidence":"medium","cautions":"The available taxonomy family 'duality' fits only broadly; the passage's emphasis is dependence and union rather than a mythic pair."},{"id":"motif:4","label":"Disembodied soul exposed to air and winds","taxonomy_refs":[],"basis":"The passage imagines mind and soul without body in open air or winds, but argues they cannot live or retain sensory motions there.","evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:7"],"confidence":"medium","cautions":"The motif is framed negatively: the passage generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"Wherefore it seems that soul\n     Hath both a natal and funeral hour.","summary":"The passage argues that vital sense and soul are distributed throughout the body, are divided or dissolved when the body is divided or dies, do not preserve memories of a prior life, and therefore have both birth and death.","language":"English","quote_policy":"quoted"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The passage states that vital sense is in the whole body and that a body cleft in two would have its soul divided along with it.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The passage states that what is severed and divided into parts does not possess an everlasting nature.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"War chariots with scythes are described as cutting off limbs suddenly; severed limbs quiver, and wounded fighters may continue acting without noticing the loss.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"A severed head is described as keeping a living countenance and open eyes until the remnants of soul are rendered up.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"A serpent cut into many parts is described as having severed fragments that writhe, spatter the ground, and the forepart seeks the hinder part with its jaws.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The passage rejects the idea that each severed fraction contains a whole soul and instead states that one soul has been divided with the body.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"A dying person is described as losing vital sense gradually: nails and toes turn blue, feet and legs die, and cold death moves over the rest.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The passage says the soul is torn, does not mount away entire, and is rent and scattered forth.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The passage considers and rejects the supposition that the soul can draw itself inward to one place in the body, noting that no such place shows greater sense.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The passage argues that if an immortal soul entered the body at birth, people should remember something of a prior life, but they do not.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The passage says that if recollection of prior deeds has wholly fallen away, this condition is not far removed from death.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The passage imagines mind powers being inserted at birth and crossing the sills of life, but says they would then live as if alone in a cavern rather than growing with limbs and blood.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The body is described as thronged with sense; soul is entwined through veins, flesh, sinews, bones, and even teeth share sensation.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The passage states that a soul entering from outside could not cleave to the frame and later leave whole and unscathed from sinews, joints, and bones.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"The passage compares a soul that seeps and soaks into the body to food dispersed through pores, saying it will be dissolved and die.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"The passage concludes that soul has both a natal hour and a funeral hour.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"speaking philosophical voice","description":"The voice presenting the argument in first person plural and first person singular, including hypothetical concessions.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"second-person addressee","description":"The addressed 'thou' in hypothetical examples and objections about the soul.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"dismembered combatants","description":"Men in the battlefield examples whose arms, shield, leg, foot, or head are separated from the body.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"serpent","description":"A serpent with darting tongue and lashing tail that is hewn into many parts, leaving with it, entwined with tissues, fused, dissolved, born, and dying.","role_refs":["role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:6","ev:7","ev:8"]}],"roles":[{"id":"role:1","label":"arguer or the soul.","evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:5"]},{"id":"role:3","label":"dismemberment example","assigned_to":["fig:3","fig:4"],"basis":"Combatants and the serpent are used as literal examples of bodily fellow exemplifies loss of vital sense by stages through the body.","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"role:5","label":"central debated vital principle","assigned_to":["fig:6"],"basis":"The passage It compares death with pre-birth nonexperience and sleep, denies posthumous sensation in a corpse, and critiques mourners who imagine loss after death.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The speaker states that death is nothing to “us” because the nature of mind is mortal.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The passage says people felt no ill in ages before birth, even amid war involving the Carthaginian host.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The passage describes death as a sundering or severance of body and soul, after which nothing can move the senses.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The passage states that even if a person’s matter were collected and set again in place with the light of life, this would not concern the former person once the self-succession of sense was broken.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The passage says pain or woe requires the person to be present at the same time, and that death precludes this.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"A man is described as grieving over his dead body rotting, burning, or being eaten, while imagining himself as that body and projecting his own sense into it.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The passage says that in true death there is no second self alive to sorrow for a destroyed self.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The passage lists imagined postmortem treatments: being jerked by beasts’ jaws and fangs, roasted in flames, suffocated in honey, chilled on an icy slab, or crushed by earth.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"An imagined lament says the dead person will no longer be welcomed by house, wife, and sons, or protect undertakings.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The speaker {"record_id":"batch.motif.polynesian-samoa-hundred-years-ago-turner-gutenberg-l331-l452","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/samoan/project-gutenberg/samoa-a-hundred-years-ago-turner.md","passage_locator":{"label":"CHAPTER XXII. / POLITICAL DIVISIONS AND PLACES OF NOTE ON SAVAII / CHAPTER I. / POSITION OF THE ISLANDS--EARLY VISITORS AND TRADITIONARY ORIGIN.; lines 331-452","start":"331","end":"452","translation":"Samoa, A Hundred Years Ago And Long Before","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage gives a chiefly genealogy identifying Savea as the first Malietoa, then presents several origin traditions: Space raises a head fallen from heaven into a child named All the sides of heaven; the children of Ilu and Mamao include rocks, moon, sun, sea, fresh water, and winds, with the released sea flooding the rocks while sun and moon flee upward; fire and water marry and produce the earth and its contents, followed by contests among natural beings and human emergence from maggots; Tangaloa creates heavens, earth, islands, and the cuttle-fish; Tangaloa's daughter in bird form searches the ocean for land and later witnesses worms become humans from a plant; other accounts form humans from stones, fire, Ariari, and mussels; the soul is linked to vapour, clouds, and sleep; and gods debate whether human death should be reversible or final using torch analogies.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Savea is identified as the first Malietoa, followed by twenty-three generations down to Malietoa Talavou.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Space, or Valevalenoa, is born from Tangaloa the explorer of lands and Queen of earth, and has a long-legged seat.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"A head said to have fallen from the heavens is set by Space on a high stool, and a body of a man-child suddenly appears with it.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The child asks who his father is; Space answers by pointing to east, west, sea-ward, inland, above, and below.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The child names himself All the sides of heaven, and the four divisions East, West, North, and South spring from him.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"All the sides of heaven goes to the North, South, East, and West, marries and has children in each direction, then goes up to the heavens and tells all his children to follow him.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Ilu, worm, and Mamao, distant, have sons named as kinds of rocks, the moon, the sun, the sea, and fresh water, and daughters named Great wind and Gentle wind.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The sea is initially shut up; when it is set free, the three kinds of rocks are flooded and die, while the sun and moon flee to the heavens and live.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Fire and water marry, and from them spring the earth, rocks, trees, and everything.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"A sequence of contests occurs among cuttle-fish, fire, rocks, stones, grass, trees, and creepers; creepers rot, swarm with maggots, and the maggots become men.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Tangaloa exists in space, makes the heavens, makes the earth under the heavens, and is associated with island formation by stones from heaven or by a fishing-hook from under the ocean.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Tangaloa makes the Fee or cuttle-fish, sends it under the earth, and the lower regions are called sacred to the cuttle-fish; the cuttle-fish brings forth rocks.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Tangaloa sends his daughter in the form of the bird Turī to search for land over an ocean with no resting-place.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The bird reports stages of land emergence, and later Tangaloa sends her with earth and a creeping plant; the plant grows, withers, swarms with worms or maggots, and the maggots become men and women.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Ants and small coral make content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.polynesian-samoa-hundred-years-ago-turner-gutenberg-l2643-l2762","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/samoan/project-gutenberg/samoa-a-hundred-years-ago-turner.md","passage_locator":{"label":"CHAPTER VI. / THE PEOPLE--INFANCY AND CHILDHOOD. / CHAPTER VII. / ADULT AND ADVANCED YEARS.; lines 2643-2762","start":"2643","end":"2762","translation":"Samoa, A Hundred Years Ago And Long Before","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage describes Samoan marriage-related customs concerning concubinage, polygamy, divorce, and widows, including kin obligations, dowry property, remarriage limits, and widow succession by a deceased husband's brother or relative. It then gives a love song in which two sisters wish for a brother, later meet the beautiful Maluafiti, bottle his liquid shadow, take it to Fiji, are mistreated by Sina, and pour the shadow into bathing water; Sina sees the image, declares the unseen man her husband, and summons villagers to identify him.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A newly married woman is attended by her brother's daughter, described as a concubine; the brother is said to risk failing in duty and offending the household god if he does not supply her.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Concubines bring _tonga_ as dowry, may live with the husband or not after presenting it, and may be added with ceremonies resembling regular marriage.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"A chief's friends may urge repeated marriages because the ceremonies bring festivities and profit, and they may pursue matches in wealthy families regardless of the daughter's preference.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Under the described system a chief might quickly have many wives and concubines, but quarrels and jealousy often lead women back to their parental homes, making more than two co-resident wives rare.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"When a marriage was contracted chiefly for property and festivities, the wife might return to her parents after only days or weeks.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"For a mutually agreed formal separation, the couple discusses the matter, divides property, and the wife returns to her friends with young children while older children remain with their father.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"A separated woman is not allowed to remarry while her husband lives, and after the death of a high-ranking chief husband she requires permission from his family; violation can bring death or a heavy fine.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"A deceased husband's brother is described as entitled to the widow and as becoming father to the orphan children; if there are several brothers, they arrange which brother will act for the deceased.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The stated reason for the widow custom is to keep the woman and children from returning to her friends and thereby preserve the number and influence of the husband's family; if no relative or the widow is willing, she may return to her own friends.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"In the love song, Tafitofau and Ongafau have two daughters, Sinaleuuna and Sinaeteva, who wish they had a brother; Ongafau later has a boy, but the sisters live apart from him.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The boy is named Maluafiti, translated in the passage as “Shade of Fiji”; when he brings food to the sisters, they are struck by his beauty, learn he is their brother, and rejoice.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The sisters fill a bamboo bottle with the liquid shadow of their brother.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"After hearing of the beautiful lady Sina in Fiji and her many pursuers, Sinaleuuna and Sinaeteva travel to Fiji with Maluafiti's shadow.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The sisters dress up and tell Sina about their handsome brother, but Sina mistreats them; Sina does not know they are Maluafiti's sisters and already longs for his coming.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"After continued ill treatment, the sisters go to the water where Sina is bathing and pour their brother's shadow from the bottle onto the water.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Sina sees the shadow in the water, is struck by its beauty, and declares the person represented to be her husband wherever she can find him.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Sina calls villagers and beautiful young men to assemble and determine whose image appears groups.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A Fijian Banian tree is reported to have defeated other trees, prompting the Samoan Tatangia axe.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The owl rewards Tasi by declaring that Tasi, previously last, will be first in numbering, while Sefulu, previously first, stands upright.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"The story says bananas formerly held their heads erect, but after quarreling and fighting with the plantain, The king tries to thwart this by taking the child and ordering his drowning, but the baby survives in a basket on the river, is rescued and adopted by a fisherman and his wife, and is named Plavacek. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-sixty-folk-tales-slavonic-wratislaw-gutenberg-l6116-l6205","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/sixty-folk-tales-slavonic-wratislaw.md","passage_locator":{"label":"XXXV.--THE LORD GOD AS AN OLD MAN. / XXXVI.--BULGARIAN HOSPITALITY. / XXXVII.--CINDERELLA. / XXXVIII.--THE GOLDEN APPLES AND THE NINE PEAHENS.; lines 6116-6205","start":"6116","end":"6205","translation":"Sixty Folk-Tales from Exclusively Slavonic Sources","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"After marriage, the empress leaves on a journey and gives the prince keys to twelve cellars, warning him about the twelfth. He opens it, gives water to a voice in an iron-hooped cask, and thereby releases a dragon, who carries off the empress. The prince seeks her, rescues a fish, fox, and crow, receiving tokens from each, then reaches the dragon emperor's palace with help from a man. He and the empress attempt to flee, but the dragon's speaking horse helps the dragon overtake them; the dragon spares the prince once because of the water given in the cellar. The prince returns, and the empress learns from the dragon that a hill-dwelling old woman has twelve horses, including a skinny but best horse able to fly to the sky, obtainable only by successfully watching a mare for three days and nights under penalty of death. The prince sets out for the old woman's hill as the passage ends.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The empress gives the prince keys to On the return journey, the man relays the answers: the stream tries to drown him after learning the cause, a cattle owner restores fertility by slaughtering his best ox on his name-day, and another content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.slavic-sixty-folk-tales-slavonic-wratislaw-gutenberg-l8174-l8262","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/slavic/project-gutenberg/sixty-folk-tales-slavonic-wratislaw.md","passage_locator":{"label":"XLVIII.--GOD'S COCK. / XLIX.--KURENT THE PRESERVER. / L.--KURENT AND MAN. / LI.--THE HUNDRED-LEAVED ROSE.; lines 8174-8262","start":"8174","end":"8262","translation":"Sixty Folk-Tales from Exclusively Slavonic Sources","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text; supplied passage text contains LI.--THE HUNDRED-LEAVED ROSE and ends mid-sentence."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The man and Kurent contend for the earth, reshaping its surface through their struggle. Dobrin briefly binds them and rules, but they overpower him and hand him to a fiery dragon. Kurent describes the hundred-leaved rose, a mysterious plant whose roots imprison living fire and whose top contains lightning and thunder. Its petals sing, regrow, and are used as an arbiter for alternating rulership. The first consultation grants rule to neither; the second grants rule to the man, who sleeps through his term. Kurent then wakes him and begins his own rule as the passage breaks off.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The man and Kurent contend for the earth and struggle together for seven years without either overcoming the other.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"During their struggle, their heels dig ravines and pile up mountains and hills where there had been plains.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"When exhausted, the man and Kurent fall like dead corpses and lie for a hundred and a hundred years.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Dobrin comes to earth, binds both sleepers, and rules the world.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The man and Kurent wake, break Dobrin's cords, bind Dobrin with golden fetters, and hand him over to a fiery dragon for service to the lady-dragon.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Kurent warns that renewed quarrelling could allow a being stronger than Dobrin to conquer both heroes.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Kurent says his garden contains a mysterious hundred-leaved rose whose root reaches the bottom of the earth and imprisons a terrible creature called living fire.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Kurent says that pulling up the rose would release living fire, turning the earth and everything in it into a desert where water has dried up.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Kurent says that seizing the top of the rose would release lightning and thunder, destroying the earth and what is above and below it, while the rose alone would remain until a new earth and race arose after a very long time.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Kurent says the petals of the rose comfort him, sing sweetly, can be plucked without danger, and regrow by the next morning.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Kurent says he learned how the stars and moon go round by watching the petals fall and rise at night.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Kurent proposes that he and the man pluck petals in an agreed order to determine who will rule the earth for one hour of God, equal to one hundred terrestrial years.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"At the first consultation, the last remaining petal belongs to neither hero, so neither is destined to rule or humble himself at that time.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"At the second consultation, the man pulls the last petal, Kurent A man lowered into the cavern encounters the Vila and Marko; Marko tests worldly strength through a red-hot iron substituted by the Vila, sends a sealed letter to the lords, and the lords suppress it out of fear that Marko may return. Mr. Spider and the Other Beef: West African Folk Tales","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Introductory editorial passage describing how Miss Cronise collected Sierra Leone oral tales at Rotifunk, the narrators and recording methods used, the perceived traditional character and abundance of the tales, and the social function of the stories as entertainment and imaginative refuge.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The collection from which the volume was selected was made by Miss Cronise while she was a teacher in the mission school at Rotifunk in Sierra Leone.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The stories were first collected without intention of publication, with an initial motive of better understanding the people she was to instruct.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The tales were gathered from mission children, many from inland homes, and from adult mission employees.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The editors state that the stories show touches of English influence but are believed to be characteristically native in essentials.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The same stories were reportedly heard from different persons and under different circumstances, which the editors present as evidence of traditional lore.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The passage says that the existence of a distinct oral literature was discovered only after considerable time among the people.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The collection methods included gaining trust, offering inducements to children, eliciting remembered stories, overhearing children’s evening talk, and inducing adults to relate stories.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The narratives were taken down literally, word for word, by rapid abbreviated writing.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Two years of work produced one hundred and twenty-five distinct stories, with the editors believing many more were current among the people.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The passage says that young mission children already possessed salient features of many stories before being taken from their people.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The stories are described as a chief source of entertainment for both children and adults.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The passage describes the legends and fables as leisure diversion, wish-fulfilling representation, entertainment, and ideal refuge from hard realities.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Miss Mr. Spider and the Other Beef: West African Folk Tales","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"A comparison of Mr. Spider and Brer Rabbit reveals many similarities and some differences","summary":"The introduction compares Temne figures such as Mr. Spider and Cunning Rabbit with Brer Rabbit, Annancy, Hlakanyana, and other animal figures, describes Cunning Rabbit as a water deerlet, and notes several parallel tale patterns including Wax Girl/Tar Baby, riding a predator, strength contests, and feigned death as a ruse.","language":"English","quote_policy":"quoted"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The passage states that Spider occupies a comparable place in West African folklore to Brer Rabbit in southern U.S. Black tales, Annancy in West Indian stories, and Hlakanyana in South African stories.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The passage reports an earlier claim of essential identity between Brer Rabbit and Hlakanyana and says there is perhaps a closer parallel between the Temne Spider and Annancy.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Mr. Spider and Brer Rabbit are both described as clever, but Brer Rabbit is characterized as more harmless in mischief, while Mr. Spider's cunning can be vicious and can bring him grief without destroying him.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Cunning Rabbit is described as rivaling Mr. Spider in shrewdness and wit and as usually having the advantage when their interests clash.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Cunning Rabbit is identified by the authors as not actually a rabbit but as the water deerlet or chevrotain, described as nimble, shy, fleet, cunning, and venerated by local people.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"A submitted skeletal fragment was identified as belonging to Hyomoschus Aquaticus, an animal said to be peculiar to West Africa.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The authors call it conjectural, but suggest a possible transfer of Cunning Rabbit's qualities to the American hare because of similarity in popular names.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"When asked where the stories came from, informants reportedly answered that they came from far up country, implying remote origin in space and time.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The passage says many stories in the collection are almost identical with tales in the Uncle Remus series and with some Annancy stories, and also resemble tales from American Indian folklore and other African Black communities.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The passage states that the Tar Baby story appears in this collection as the Wax Girl and that the encounter is the same in the Spider/Wax Girl and Brer Rabbit/Tar Baby versions, though preliminaries and outcomes differ.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:10","ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Brer
